title: The Story of an Hour
focus: a woman's brief taste of freedom

teacherSummary.text: Told gently that her husband Brently has died in a railroad accident, Louise Mallard weeps, then alone in her room feels a growing, monstrous joy: 'Free, free, free!' She looks ahead to years that will belong to herself. Leaving the room, she sees Brently walk in the door, unharmed; he had not been on the train. She dies, and the doctors say of 'the joy that kills'.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the story for irony, imagery (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this story suggest about a woman's brief taste of freedom? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how The Story of an Hour develops the idea of a woman's brief taste of freedom. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and imagery shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Chopin uses irony to show that Louise's death comes from lost freedom, not joy. When the text says “of the joy that kills” (The Story of an Hour, paragraph 19), it shows this directly. She whispers "Free! Body and soul free!", and when her husband returns the doctors say she died "of the joy that kills," a diagnosis the reader knows is wrong.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Death; marriage as constraint. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. No; she was drinking in a very elixir of life through that o…”). Treat it as period custom or plot detail; name it plainly and don't glamorize it.
